Development guide

Introduction

The EDS AI-Software Development Lifecycle (AI-SDLC) guides teams from user research through software development, testing and release. This guide explains where AI can help and where people review results and make decisions.

Target audience

This guide is for in-house development squads within EDS. It gives developers a shared reference for using AI to understand problems, explore solutions, build software and check outcomes.

The guide covers AI-assisted development: work supported by AI tools, whether or not the product itself contains AI.

Why AI-SDLC?

Product development has traditionally been organised around limited specialist capacity. Product management, research, design, engineering, testing, security and operations each have their own priorities, tools and pace, so the lifecycle sequences their effort carefully.

Work passes from opportunity to requirements, design, build, test, approval and launch before the team learns from users. Each arrow is a handoff where work can wait, lose context or be reinterpreted. The dashed path shows that evidence from users returns only after most of the effort has been spent.

Agile, DevOps, continuous delivery and design thinking improved this model through smaller batches and faster feedback. Much of the work is still limited by specialist capacity, handoffs and the cost of changing direction.

AI can help teams draft requirements, build prototypes, write code and run checks with less manual effort. AI-SDLC brings these capabilities into the whole development workflow, with people setting goals, reviewing evidence and deciding what to release. The aim is faster validated learning: testing assumptions early and using the results to decide what to build or change.

  1. Reduce delays between specialists

    Work can stall while a designer waits for clarification, a developer waits for design or a security reviewer waits for architecture. AI can turn shared requirements into draft screens, test cases and questions for security review, giving specialists material to review together earlier.

    Give the AI tool the same requirements, constraints and recorded decisions that the team uses. Product, engineering and security specialists review the drafts, resolve conflicting assumptions and record decisions before dependent work proceeds.

  2. Test assumptions before committing

    Finding that users do not need a solution after months of development can mean substantial rework. AI can help build a small prototype and draft test tasks, reducing the effort needed to put an idea in front of users.

    Choose an assumption that could change the product decision, then test it with users before building the full solution. Use AI to organise the findings, check the summary against the original observations and decide whether to continue, revise or stop.

  3. Explore more options before choosing

    When each alternative takes substantial effort to produce, teams may settle on the first plausible design. AI can draft several interface designs or implementation approaches from the same requirements, making alternatives easier to compare.

    Ask for options with different trade-offs, then test them against the same user needs, constraints and success criteria. Designers and engineers review feasibility and test results before selecting an approach or combining useful parts.

  4. Revise or replace unsuitable code

    Teams can spend more effort patching an unsuitable implementation than trying a different approach. An AI agent can help rewrite a small component and run its regression tests, reducing the manual effort of comparing a replacement.

    Give the agent the required behaviour, interface contracts and tests that the replacement needs to pass. Developers review the changes and test results, then decide whether the replacement improves the solution enough to justify switching.

    Note

    Some decisions remain costly to reverse: core data models, public APIs, regulatory commitments, major architecture choices, vendor dependencies, user migrations and security models. Make these deliberately, with human judgement.

  5. Improve the whole delivery workflow

    AI can produce requirements, code and prototypes faster than the team can review them. If review, testing and user feedback cannot keep pace, work accumulates at the next step and delivery still waits.

    Illustrative examples of how faster tasks can move the bottleneck
    Faster taskIf the rest stays the sameLikely result
    AI drafts more product requestsEngineering capacity is unchangedThe engineering queue can grow
    AI helps developers write code fasterSecurity review capacity is unchangedChanges can queue for security review
    AI helps build prototypes fasterUser testing still takes months to arrangeThe team still waits to learn whether the solution helps

    An agent harness provides instructions, tools and checks for AI to carry out tasks. Use it to connect development work with automated tests, policy checks and review steps.

    Track where work waits, arrange user testing early and improve the slowest step before increasing the volume of generated work.

  6. Check AI outputs as work progresses

    AI can generate code, designs and tests in large volumes, increasing the amount of work that needs checking. An agent harness can run tests and scanners after each change, giving developers feedback while the work is still easy to revise.

    Define the expected behaviour and checks before the agent starts. When a check fails, use the result to correct the work or reconsider the approach.

    Developers review generated tests against the requirements, and relevant specialists assess usability, security and other areas that need judgement. Keep the results with the change so reviewers can see why it is ready to proceed.

  7. Measure time to an informed decision

    AI can increase the number of prototypes, tests and code changes a team produces. Those counts alone do not show whether the team has resolved an important uncertainty or improved an outcome for users.

    Track the time and cost of testing an assumption and reaching a decision. Compare AI-assisted work with the team's previous approach, including the effort spent reviewing, correcting and testing generated outputs.

    Example: use AI to build a prototype of a clearer upload flow. Test whether at least 8 of 10 pilot users can submit the right document unaided, with no wrong-recipient uploads. Record the preparation, review and testing effort alongside the results. If the agreed threshold is met, commit to a bounded implementation; otherwise revise the flow or stop.

    Use each decision to choose the next experiment. Check whether AI is helping the team reach useful decisions sooner and whether the resulting changes improve users' experience.

An evergreen development guide

This site is an evergreen guide for EDS developers: a reference to return to as the squad’s work progresses, rather than a document read once. It explains AI-SDLC practices so they can be applied in day-to-day development.

The guidance is expected to change as tools develop and squads gain experience. Each practice records its reasons, so the advice can be revisited when the evidence changes.

To begin, pick one assumption in your current work that would be costly to get wrong. Agree what evidence would help the squad decide, then choose a small experiment to obtain it.
